Multistability of Self-Attention Dynamics in Transformers

Claudio Altafini ††thanks: C. Altafini is with the Division of Automatic Control, Dept. of Electrical Engineering, Linköping University, SE-58183, Linköping, Sweden. email: claudio.altafini@liu.se. Work supported in part by the Swedish Research Council (grant n. 2024-04772) and by the ELLIIT framework program at Linköping University.
Abstract

In machine learning, a self-attention dynamics is a continuous-time multiagent-like model of the attention mechanisms of transformers. In this paper we show that such dynamics is related to a multiagent version of the Oja flow, a dynamical system that computes the principal eigenvector of a matrix corresponding for transformers to the value matrix. We classify the equilibria of the “single-head” self-attention system into four classes: consensus, bipartite consensus, clustering and polygonal equilibria. Multiple asymptotically stable equilibria from the first three classes often coexist in the self-attention dynamics. Interestingly, equilibria from the first two classes are always aligned with the eigenvectors of the value matrix, often but not exclusively with the principal eigenvector.

1 Introduction

Less than a decade since their introduction [27], transformer architectures have become the de facto standard algorithm for many problems in machine learning and are widely adopted in various fields, such as natural language processing, computer vision and speech processing [13, 28, 12]. At the core of a transformer is a so-called self-attention mechanism, a set of operations performed on vectorial representations of the “tokens” i.e., elementary units of the objects under analysis (words for large language models (LLM), images patches in computer vision, etc.). These operations involve three matrices called query (QQ), key (KK) and value (OPENV)V) matrices, two of which, QQ and KK, are involved in an inner product, which, exponentiated and normalized by a partition function, yields a softmax function depending on the tokens. Such softmax function is the celebrated attention mechanism, and expresses how much attention a token ii is giving to another token jj, relative to the ensemble of all tokens. The attention coefficients provide the weight in the weighted sum of the product of the tokens by the value matrix VV, hence forming a “self-attention” mechanism. This is the core of a transformer layer, which receives as input the tokens and gives as output “transformed” tokens. To avoid a collapsing or exploding token norm due to these operations, the output is then normalized. Other operations (which we do not consider here) are typically present, like for instance multiple such mechanisms act simultaneously to form a “multi-head” attention, or the output just described is passed through a feedforward neural network. Overall this mechanism constitutes a layer of the transformer: multiple identical layers are concatenated to form what is normally referred to as a transformer.

As is often the case in machine learning, the mathematical understanding of a new approach (“why it works”) lags behind its practical use, and transformer are no exception [26]. However, given the incredible importance in everyday life that transformer-based applications like LLM are acquiring, investigating and understanding their behavior from a rational perspective appears an important and compelling issue.

One possible approach to investigating the behavior of transformers was provided recently in a series of papers [6, 21, 14, 7, 8, 11, 29]. The basic idea of these papers is to treat the repeated application of identical layers typical of a transformer as the unfolding in time of a dynamical system whose states are the tokens being modified by each transformer layer. Rather than dealing with a discrete-time dynamical system (as the setting would immediately suggest), [7, 8] opt for passing to a continuous-time description, which is more amenable to mathematical analysis and easier to characterize. The resulting ODE model corresponds to a transformer with an infinite number of layers, which is clearly an idealization (in practical implementations, a transformer may have tens or hundreds of layers). An interesting perspective that is suggested in [7, 8] is that such ODE can be seen as a multiagent dynamical system, in which each agent (called a “particle” in [7, 8]) is a token, and its update law depends on all the other tokens/agents. The resulting dynamics is nonlinear due to the attention mechanism, and evolves on a unit sphere because of the normalization operation.

Multiagent systems on spheres have been studied extensively in the control community [3, 16, 25, 33, 34], in particular for what concerns colletive phenomena like consensus (all agents converge to the same point in the unit sphere) and more complex, yet related, behaviors like bipartite consensus (when some agents converge to a common point and some other to the antipodal point [3, 33]) which appear naturally because of the compact nature of the ambient manifold. These collective behaviors are highly relevant for transformers: it has in fact been observed repeatedly that transformers indeed tend to be subject to rank-collapse phenomena [4, 18] (also sometimes referred to as token-uniformity or over-smoothing [17, 23, 24, 32, 5]) which appear essentially when the tokens become equal or cluster into groups of equal tokens. Indeed in [7, 8] consensus is one of the main behaviors shown to occur for this continuous-time model of self-attention dynamics. A similar result is reported in [1] (paper which is closest to ours in terms of mathematical approach).

The scope of this paper is to make a thorough analysis of the asymptotic behavior of the continous-time self-attention dynamics model of [7, 8] using tools from dynamical systems and control. In order to do so we establish a connection with another well-know model on the sphere, which, following [19, 20, 9, 30, 31], we call the Oja flow, but which is also related to the continuous-time Rayleigh quotient flow [9] and to the continuous-time power method, see eq. (3) of [15]. This is a much simpler dynamical system whose main feature is that it converges to the principal eigenvector of a matrix which in our setting corresponds to the value matrix VV. In fact, Oja flows are at the basis of algorithms that are used to compute the eigenvectors of a matrix, and have long been used for this scope as an alternative to power methods e.g. in principal component analysis [10, 22]. The Oja flow is insightful but far too simple to use for the self-attention dynamics. However a multiagent version of Oja flow, which we develop in the paper, is much more similar, and in fact it corresponds to the self-attention dynamics without the attention coefficients. Similarly to the Oja flow, the multiagent Oja flow discovers the principal eigenvector of the value matrix VV, i.e., all agents converge to a consensus equilibrium which is aligned with the principal eigenvector of VV. In addition, the consensus and bipartite consensus points aligned with the other eigenvectors of VV are also equilibria, but always unstable. It can be shown explicitly that the multiagent Oja flow generically converges to consensus at the principal eigenvector of VV.

The self-attention dynamics is obtained inserting an attention matrix in the multiagent Oja flow, and corresponds to replacing a constant average coupling among the agents (equal for all agents) with a weighted average coupling, which is varying from agent to agent and over time. Even restricting to time-invariant QQ, KK and VV, and to symmetric VV, the asymptotic behavior changes significantly w.r.t. the multiagent Oja flow: while consensus at the principal eigenvector still remains a locally asymptotically stable equilibrium point, other locally asymptotically stable equilibria normally emerge, rendering the typical self-attention dynamics multistable. Most of the new attractors correspond to bipartite consensus equilibria, aligned with the principal eigenvector or with some other eigenvector of VV, even though sometimes other locally stable equilibria, which we call clustering equilibria, may emerge. The name derives from the (numerical) observation that, just like consensus and bipartite consensus, even these extra equilibria are typically in the form of clusters of tokens, i.e., multiple tokens end-up in the same point on the sphere. All these equilibria correspond to low-rank attention matrices: rank-1 (uniform) for consensus, rank-2 for a bipartite consensus, and typically low rank also for the clustering equilibria. The complete classification of equilibria of the self-attention dynamics includes also the so-called polygonal equilibria [3], which are however always unstable. Bipartite consensus and clustering equilibria are not mentioned in papers like [1, 2], which focus only on consensus. While the stability properties of the consensus and bipartite consensus equilibria can be studied analytically through the Lyapunov indirect method, as we do in this paper, for the more complex clustering equilibria an analytical treatment seems still out of reach.

While convergence towards a consensus-type of equilibrium is known both experimentally and theoretically, the observation that convergence typically occurs towards one of the eigenvectors of the value matrix does not seem to appear in the literature11 1 With the exception of [1], where asymptotic stability to a consensus aligned with the principal eigenvector of VV is shown, but only for an autoregressive model, i.e., a model with a triangular attention matrix.. Often the consensus or bipartite consensus aligns with the principal eigenvector of VV, as in a multiagent Oja flow, but alignment with other eigenvectors of VV can also occur, in particular with the one corresponding to the least (i.e., most negative) eigenvalue. This asymptotic behavior can be considered a form of nonlinear Perron-Frobenius property, and it might provide insight into the interpretation of a transformer, potentially verifiable on real data with pretrained transformer matrices.

2 Model formulation

Consider nn tokens represented as unit length vectors 𝒙i∈𝕊d−1⊂ℝd\bm{x}_{i}\in\mathbb{S}^{d-1}\subset\mathbb{R}^{d}, i=1,…,ni=1,\ldots,n. Denote Q,K∈ℝm×dQ,K\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times d} the query and key matrices (for simplicity and without loss of generality we hereafter assume m=dm=d) and V∈ℝd×dV\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d} the value matrix.

Following [8], an ODE model for a single-head self-attention mechanism on nn tokens can be formulated as follows

𝒙˙i=(I−𝒙i​𝒙iT)​∑j=1ne⟨Q​𝒙i,K​𝒙j⟩∑ℓ=1ne⟨Q​𝒙i,K​𝒙ℓ⟩​V​𝒙j=(I−𝒙i𝒙iT)V∑j=1nAi​j(x)𝒙j,i=1,…,n\begin{split}\dot{\bm{x}}_{i}&=(I-\bm{x}_{i}\bm{x}_{i}^{T})\sum_{j=1}^{n}\frac{e^{\langle Q\bm{x}_{i},K\bm{x}_{j}\rangle}}{\sum_{\ell=1}^{n}e^{\langle Q\bm{x}_{i},K\bm{x}_{\ell}\rangle}}V\bm{x}_{j}\\ &=(I-\bm{x}_{i}\bm{x}_{i}^{T})V\sum_{j=1}^{n}A_{ij}(x)\bm{x}_{j},\qquad i=1,\ldots,n\end{split} (1)

where for the terms of (1) we have the following interpretation:

    Pi=(I−𝒙i​𝒙iT)P_{i}=(I-\bm{x}_{i}\bm{x}_{i}^{T}) is the projection onto T𝒙i​𝕊d−1T_{\bm{x}_{i}}\mathbb{S}^{d-1}, the tangent space of 𝕊d−1\mathbb{S}^{d-1} at 𝒙i\bm{x}_{i}. This guarantees that ‖𝒙i​(t)‖=1\|\bm{x}_{i}(t)\|=1 for all tt, i.e., that the flow of (1) evolves on the unit sphere 𝕊d−1\mathbb{S}^{d-1}. In fact, for any 𝒚∈𝕊d−1\bm{y}\in\mathbb{S}^{d-1}, Pi​𝒚=(I−𝒙i​𝒙iT)​𝒚=𝒚−⟨𝒙i,𝒚⟩​𝒙iP_{i}\bm{y}=(I-\bm{x}_{i}\bm{x}_{i}^{T})\bm{y}=\bm{y}-\langle\bm{x}_{i},\bm{y}\rangle\bm{x}_{i} is always normal to 𝒙i\bm{x}_{i}, and 𝒙iT​𝒙˙i=0\bm{x}_{i}^{T}\dot{\bm{x}}_{i}=0. The projection models the layer normalization present on each layer of the transformer.

  • •

    Ai​j​(𝒙)=e⟨Q​𝒙i,K​𝒙j⟩∑ℓ=1ne⟨Q​𝒙i,K​𝒙ℓ⟩A_{ij}(\bm{x})=\frac{e^{\langle Q\bm{x}_{i},K\bm{x}_{j}\rangle}}{\sum_{\ell=1}^{n}e^{\langle Q\bm{x}_{i},K\bm{x}_{\ell}\rangle}} is the attention that the token 𝒙i\bm{x}_{i} gives to the token 𝒙j\bm{x}_{j}, computed through a softmax function (𝒙\bm{x} is the stack of 𝒙1,…,𝒙n\bm{x}_{1},\ldots,\bm{x}_{n} vectors). Ai​j​(𝒙)A_{ij}(\bm{x}) is a nonnegative scalar. The attention matrix is then A​(𝒙)=[Ai​j​(𝒙)]A(\bm{x})=[A_{ij}(\bm{x})] and it is a row stochastic matrix, i.e., A⁡(𝒙)​𝟙=𝟙A(\bm{x})\mathds{1}=\mathds{1}.

  • •

    In the model (1) time corresponds to the layer index, hence a self-attention model in continuous-time can be interpreted as a “continuum of layers”. The asymptotic value of the ODE, 𝒙i​(∞)\bm{x}_{i}(\infty), corresponds to the output of a transformer with an infinite number of layers.

The model (1) represents each token 𝒙i\bm{x}_{i} as an “agent” (it is called a “particle” in [8]) evolving on the sphere 𝕊d−1\mathbb{S}^{d-1}. The total state space is given by 𝒙=[𝒙1T…𝒙nT]T∈(𝕊d−1)n\bm{x}=\begin{bmatrix}\bm{x}_{1}^{T}&\ldots&\bm{x}_{n}^{T}\end{bmatrix}^{T}\in(\mathbb{S}^{d-1})^{n}. Since the flow of (1) lies on the compact manifold (𝕊d−1)n(\mathbb{S}^{d-1})^{n}, the vector field is Lipschitz, so forward existence, uniqueness and boundedness for all tt follow automatically.

The model (1) corresponds to an example of collective dynamics on the sphere similar to those investigated in e.g. [3, 16, 33, 34]: the evolution occurs on a product of unit spheres and it is driven by the interaction with the other agents. The difference with these other models of collective dynamics on the sphere is that in (1) the attention matrix A⁡(𝒙)A(\bm{x}) provides the “interaction graph”. It is typically fully connected and time-varying, since it depends on 𝒙\bm{x}.

We are interested in studying the dynamical behavior of (1), and in particular in investigating its equilibria and their stability properties. To do so, we exploit the fact that the model (1) has some similarities with the so-called Oja flow, reviewed in next Section, and especially with a multiagent version of Oja flow, investigated in Section 4.

3 Oja flow

In its simplest formulation, the Oja flow [19, 20, 9] is the following dynamical system

𝒙˙=(I−𝒙​𝒙T)​V​𝒙,𝒙∈𝕊d−1.\dot{\bm{x}}=(I-\bm{x}\bm{x}^{T})V\bm{x},\qquad\bm{x}\in\mathbb{S}^{d-1}. (2)

Assume that VV is symmetric of eigenvalues λ1>λ2≥…≥λd\lambda_{1}>\lambda_{2}\geq\ldots\geq\lambda_{d}, with λ1\lambda_{1} simple, and 𝒗1,…,𝒗d\bm{v}_{1},\ldots,\bm{v}_{d} the associated eigenvectors, normalized s.t. ‖𝒗k‖=1\|\bm{v}_{k}\|=1. The dynamical behavior of (2) is summarized in the next lemma. Consider the Rayleigh quotient R⁡(𝒙)=𝒙T​V​𝒙‖𝒙‖2R(\bm{x})=\frac{\bm{x}^{T}V\bm{x}}{\|\bm{x}\|^{2}}, which on the unit sphere reduces to the quadratic form R⁡(𝒙)=𝒙T​V​𝒙R(\bm{x})=\bm{x}^{T}V\bm{x}. R⁡(𝒙)R(\bm{x}) can be used to construct a Lyapunov function for (2).

Lemma 1

All eigenvectors 𝐯k\bm{v}_{k} of VV (more precisely, the values ±𝐯k\pm\bm{v}_{k}, ‖𝐯k‖=1\|\bm{v}_{k}\|=1) are equilibria of (2). The function W⁡(𝐱)=12​(λ1−R⁡(𝐱))W(\bm{x})=\frac{1}{2}(\lambda_{1}-R(\bm{x})) is a Lyapunov function for (2) and guarantees that (2) converges to the principal eigenvector ±𝐯1\pm\bm{v}_{1} of VV for almost all initial conditions 𝐱⁡(0)∈𝕊d−1\bm{x}(0)\in\mathbb{S}^{d-1}, while all other ±𝐯k\pm\bm{v}_{k}, k=2,…,dk=2,\ldots,d, are unstable.

Proof.

From λd=𝒙T​λd​𝒙≤R⁡(𝒙)≤𝒙T​λ1​𝒙=λ1\lambda_{d}=\bm{x}^{T}\lambda_{d}\bm{x}\leq R(\bm{x})\leq\bm{x}^{T}\lambda_{1}\bm{x}=\lambda_{1}, R⁡(𝒙)R(\bm{x}) is upper bounded by λ1\lambda_{1} on 𝕊d−1\mathbb{S}^{d-1}, hence W⁡(𝒙)≥0W(\bm{x})\geq 0 and W⁡(𝒙)=0W(\bm{x})=0 only when 𝒙=±𝒗1\bm{x}=\pm\bm{v}_{1}, since λ1>λk\lambda_{1}>\lambda_{k} k=2,…,dk=2,\ldots,d. Differentiating, we have

W˙​(𝒙)=−𝒙T​V2​𝒙+(𝒙T​V​𝒙)2=−‖(I−𝒙​𝒙T)​V​𝒙‖2≤0\begin{split}\dot{W}(\bm{x})&=-\bm{x}^{T}V^{2}\bm{x}+(\bm{x}^{T}V\bm{x})^{2}\\ &=-\|(I-\bm{x}\bm{x}^{T})V\bm{x}\|^{2}\leq 0\end{split} (3)

with W˙​(𝒙)=0\dot{W}(\bm{x})=0 iff 𝒙=±𝒗k\bm{x}=\pm\bm{v}_{k} where 𝒗k\bm{v}_{k} is an eigenvector of VV. Also, from (3), W˙​(𝒙)=0\dot{W}(\bm{x})=0 iff (I−𝒙​𝒙T)​V​𝒙=0(I-\bm{x}\bm{x}^{T})V\bm{x}=0 i.e., V​𝒙V\bm{x} is collinear with 𝒙\bm{x}, which guarantees that the eigenvectors 𝒗k\bm{v}_{k} of VV (more precisely, on the sphere, the values ±𝒗k\pm\bm{v}_{k} with ‖𝒗k‖=1\|\bm{v}_{k}\|=1) are the equilibria of (2). From LaSalle invariance principle, the only trajectories in the level surfaces of W⁡(𝒙)W(\bm{x}) are the eigenvectors 𝒗k\bm{v}_{k} of VV, which guarantees that (3) converges to ±𝒗k\pm\bm{v}_{k} for some k=1,…,dk=1,\ldots,d.

To show convergence to the principal eigenvector 𝒗1\bm{v}_{1} of VV let us consider the linearization of (2) at 𝒗k\bm{v}_{k}. Let 𝒙=𝒗k+𝒖\bm{x}=\bm{v}_{k}+\bm{u} with 𝒖\bm{u} a small increment s.t. 𝒖T​𝒗k=0\bm{u}^{T}\bm{v}_{k}=0 (so that the linearization indeed lies in T𝒗k​𝕊d−1T_{\bm{v}_{k}}\mathbb{S}^{d-1}, the tangent plane to the unit sphere at 𝒗k\bm{v}_{k}). Computing the linearization, we get

𝒖˙=(V−λk​I)​𝒖.\dot{\bm{u}}=(V-\lambda_{k}I)\bm{u}. (4)

Expressing 𝒖\bm{u} in the eigenbasis of VV, 𝒖=∑j=1dηj​𝒗j\bm{u}=\sum_{j=1}^{d}\eta_{j}\bm{v}_{j}, then for j≠kj\neq k, we can project (4) along 𝒗j\bm{v}_{j} getting the scalar ODE η˙j=(λj−λk)​ηj.\dot{\eta}_{j}=(\lambda_{j}-\lambda_{k})\eta_{j}. If k≠1k\neq 1, then for one of the projections it must be j=1j=1. Since λ1\lambda_{1} is a strictly dominant eigenvalue, it is always λ1−λk>0\lambda_{1}-\lambda_{k}>0, i.e., each linearization of 𝒗k≠𝒗1\bm{v}_{k}\neq\bm{v}_{1} is unstable. Only when 𝒗k=𝒗1\bm{v}_{k}=\bm{v}_{1} it is λj−λ1<0\lambda_{j}-\lambda_{1}<0 for all jj, meaning that the linearization at 𝒗1\bm{v}_{1} is locally asymptotically stable. Hence (2) converges (almost always) to ±𝒗1\pm\bm{v}_{1} i.e. to the principal eigenvector of the matrix VV.  

Notice that, while convergence of ±𝒗1\pm\bm{v}_{1} is generic, also the other eigenvalues 𝒗k\bm{v}_{k}, k=2,…,dk=2,\ldots,d, have stable submanifolds of various sizes, always strictly smaller than the ambient manifold 𝕊d−1\mathbb{S}^{d-1} (and hence of measure 0).

4 Multiagent Oja flow

In this section we propose an extension of the Oja flow in the style of multiagent systems. It corresponds essentially to the self-attention system (1) without the attention matrix. Consider nn vectors 𝒙i∈𝕊d−1\bm{x}_{i}\in\mathbb{S}^{d-1} obeying the coupled ODEs:

𝒙˙i=1n(I−𝒙i𝒙iT)∑j=1nV𝒙j,i=1,…,n.\dot{\bm{x}}_{i}=\frac{1}{n}(I-\bm{x}_{i}\bm{x}_{i}^{T})\sum_{j=1}^{n}V\bm{x}_{j},\qquad i=1,\ldots,n. (5)

The key difference w.r.t. the Oja flow (2) is that in the right hand side of the ODEs the action of a single agent is replaced by the mean of the nn agents 𝒎=𝒎⁡(𝒙)=1n​∑j=1n𝒙j\bm{m}=\bm{m}(\bm{x})=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{j=1}^{n}\bm{x}_{j}.

We make the following assumption which holds throughout the rest of the paper.

Assumption 1

The value matrix V∈ℝd×dV\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d} is symmetric, of eigenvalues λ1>λ2≥…≥λd\lambda_{1}>\lambda_{2}\geq\ldots\geq\lambda_{d} with λ1>0\lambda_{1}>0 simple and positive.

Let 𝒗1,…,𝒗d\bm{v}_{1},\ldots,\bm{v}_{d} be the associated eigenvectors, normalized s.t. ‖𝒗k‖=1\|\bm{v}_{k}\|=1.

4.1 Equilibria

Let us begin by expressing the notion of consensus and bipartite consensus for multiagent systems on the sphere that will be used in this paper. The points 𝒙1,…,𝒙n∈𝕊d−1\bm{x}_{1},\ldots,\bm{x}_{n}\in\mathbb{S}^{d-1} are said to be in a consensus state if 𝒙i=𝒙j=𝒗k\bm{x}_{i}=\bm{x}_{j}=\bm{v}_{k} ∀i,j=1,…,n\forall\,i,j=1,\ldots,n and for some k=1,…,dk=1,\ldots,d. They are said to be in a bipartite consensus state if 𝒙i=±𝒙j=±𝒗k\bm{x}_{i}=\pm\bm{x}_{j}=\pm\bm{v}_{k} ∀i,j=1,…,n\forall\,i,j=1,\ldots,n and for some k=1,…,dk=1,\ldots,d.

Remark 1

W.r.t. the literature, [1, 33, 34], we expressly require a consensus or bipartite consensus point to be aligned with one of the eigenvectors of VV. This choice will be useful when we treat the self-attention dynamics in Section 5.

Let 𝒚=V​𝒎​(𝒙)=1n​V​∑j=1n𝒙j∈ℝd\bm{y}=V\bm{m}(\bm{x})=\frac{1}{n}V\sum_{j=1}^{n}\bm{x}_{j}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} be the total influence of all agents on agent ii (which is the same for all agents).

Lemma 2

The system (5) has the following classes of equilibria:

  1. 1.

    consensus: 𝒙i=𝒗k\bm{x}_{i}=\bm{v}_{k} ∀i\forall\,i, and k=1,…,dk=1,\ldots,d;

  2. 2.

    bipartite consensus: 𝒙i=±𝒗k\bm{x}_{i}=\pm\bm{v}_{k} ∀i\forall\,i and k=1,…,dk=1,\ldots,d;

  3. 3.

    polygonal equilibria: {𝒙i∈𝕊d−1s.t.V∑j=1n𝒙j=0}.\{{\bm{x}_{i}\in\mathbb{S}^{d-1}}\;\text{s.t.}\;V\sum_{j=1}^{n}\bm{x}_{j}=0\}.

Proof.

The proof follows the reasoning of [3]. Using 𝒚\bm{y}, (5) becomes

𝒙˙i=(I−𝒙i​𝒙iT)​𝒚=𝒚−𝒙i​⟨𝒙i,𝒚⟩,\dot{\bm{x}}_{i}=(I-\bm{x}_{i}\bm{x}_{i}^{T})\bm{y}=\bm{y}-\bm{x}_{i}\langle\bm{x}_{i},\bm{y}\rangle, (6)

and an equilibrium is a point 𝒙∈(𝕊d−1)n\bm{x}\in(\mathbb{S}^{d-1})^{n} in which 𝒚\bm{y} is collinear with 𝒙i\bm{x}_{i} ∀i=1,…,n\forall\,i=1,\ldots,n, or in which 𝒚\bm{y} vanishes. This can happen in 3 cases:

  1. 1.

    𝒚=γi​𝒙i\bm{y}=\gamma_{i}\bm{x}_{i}, for some scalar γi>0\gamma_{i}>0 (consensus);

  2. 2.

    𝒚=−γi​𝒙i\bm{y}=-\gamma_{i}\bm{x}_{i}, for some scalar γi>0\gamma_{i}>0 (bipartite consensus);

  3. 3.

    𝒚=0\bm{y}=0 (polygonal equilibria).

In fact, in the first two cases, (6) becomes 𝒙˙i=±γi​(𝒙i−𝒙i​𝒙iT​𝒙i)=0\dot{\bm{x}}_{i}=\pm\gamma_{i}(\bm{x}_{i}-\bm{x}_{i}\bm{x}_{i}^{T}\bm{x}_{i})=0, since 𝒙iT​𝒙i=1\bm{x}_{i}^{T}\bm{x}_{i}=1. The third case follows trivially from (6). To show that consensus must be an eigenvector of VV, observe that at this equilibrium point the total influence 𝒚\bm{y} can be written as 𝒚=V​𝒙i\bm{y}=V\bm{x}_{i}, since 𝒙i=𝒙j\bm{x}_{i}=\bm{x}_{j}. From the expression above, it is also 𝒚=γi​𝒙i\bm{y}=\gamma_{i}\bm{x}_{i}. Putting together these two expressions of 𝒚\bm{y}: V​𝒙i=γi​𝒙iV\bm{x}_{i}=\gamma_{i}\bm{x}_{i}, i.e., 𝒙i\bm{x}_{i} is an eigenvector of VV and γi\gamma_{i} one of its eigenvalues. The argument for bipartite consensus is identical.

 

For a given 𝒗k\bm{v}_{k} there are 2n2^{n} possible consensus or bipartite consensus points. These are always paired by a global symmetry w.r.t. the origin, i.e., if 𝒙i=𝒗k\bm{x}_{i}=\bm{v}_{k} ∀i\forall\,i is a consensus point, its antipodal point 𝒙i=−𝒗k\bm{x}_{i}=-\bm{v}_{k} ∀i\forall\,i is also a consensus point, and similarly for the bipartite consensus equilibria.

The name polygonal equilibria [3] is due to the observation that 𝒛j=V​𝒙j\bm{z}_{j}=V\bm{x}_{j} must sum to 0, hence they must correspond to the vertices of a spherical polygon, see also [16]. Notice that while the collinear equilibria (consensus and bipartite consensus) are isolated points in (𝕊d−1)n(\mathbb{S}^{d-1})^{n}, polygonal equilibria form instead a set. The set is of zero measure in (𝕊d−1)n(\mathbb{S}^{d-1})^{n}, as it is determined by algebraic constraints. When VV is invertible, the polygonal equilibria are the manifold {∑j=1n𝒙j=0}∩(𝕊d−1)n\{\sum_{j=1}^{n}\bm{x}_{j}=0\}\cap(\mathbb{S}^{d-1})^{n}.

4.2 Stability analysis

The following theorem summarizes the stability and convergence properties of the multiagent Oja system (5).

Theorem 1

For the system (5), under Assumption 1, the consensus equilibrium at the principal eigenvector 𝐯1\bm{v}_{1} of VV is asymptotically stable, while the other consensus equilibria 𝐯k\bm{v}_{k}, k=2,…,dk=2,\ldots,d, the bipartite consensus equilibria and the polygonal equilibria are all unstable. The trajectories of (5) converge to 𝐯1\bm{v}_{1} for almost all initial conditions 𝐱i​(0)∈(𝕊d−1)n\bm{x}_{i}(0)\in(\mathbb{S}^{d-1})^{n}.

To prove this theorem we need a series of preliminary lemmas. We start by computing the Jacobian linearization of (5). Denote fi​(𝒙)=1n​(I−𝒙i​𝒙iT)​∑j=1nV​𝒙jf_{i}(\bm{x})=\frac{1}{n}(I-\bm{x}_{i}\bm{x}_{i}^{T})\sum_{j=1}^{n}V\bm{x}_{j} and f⁡(𝒙)=[f1​(𝒙)T…fn​(𝒙)T]Tf(\bm{x})=\begin{bmatrix}f_{1}(\bm{x})^{T}&\ldots&f_{n}(\bm{x})^{T}\end{bmatrix}^{T} the (n​d)(nd)-dimensional vector field associated to the stacked state vector 𝒙=[𝒙1T…𝒙nT]T∈(𝕊d−1)n\bm{x}=\begin{bmatrix}\bm{x}_{1}^{T}&\ldots&\bm{x}_{n}^{T}\end{bmatrix}^{T}\in(\mathbb{S}^{d-1})^{n}.

Lemma 3

The Jacobian of (5), F⁡(𝐱)=∂f⁡(𝐱)∂𝐱=[∂fi​(𝐱)∂𝐱h]F(\bm{x})=\frac{\partial f(\bm{x})}{\partial\bm{x}}=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{\partial f_{i}(\bm{x})}{\partial\bm{x}_{h}}\end{bmatrix} has the following components:

  • •

    diagonal terms:

    ∂fi​(𝒙)∂𝒙i=1n​((I−𝒙i​𝒙iT)​V−∑j=1n(𝒙iT​V​𝒙j​I+𝒙i​𝒙jT​V)),\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\frac{\partial f_{i}(\bm{x})}{\partial\bm{x}_{i}}=\frac{1}{n}\Big((I-\bm{x}_{i}\bm{x}_{i}^{T})V-\sum_{j=1}^{n}\left(\bm{x}_{i}^{T}V\bm{x}_{j}I+\bm{x}_{i}\bm{x}_{j}^{T}V\right)\Big),
  • •

    off-diagonal terms: ∂fi​(𝒙)∂𝒙h=1n​(I−𝒙i​𝒙iT)​V\frac{\partial f_{i}(\bm{x})}{\partial\bm{x}_{h}}=\frac{1}{n}(I-\bm{x}_{i}\bm{x}_{i}^{T})V, h≠ih\neq i.

Proof.

For the diagonal terms direct calculations give

∂fi​(𝒙)∂𝒙i=1n(∂∂𝒙iV(∑j=1n𝒙j)−∂∂𝒙iV(𝒙i𝒙iTV∑j=1n𝒙j))=1n(V−𝒙iTV∑j=1n𝒙jI−𝒙i(𝒙iTV+∑j=1n𝒙jTV)).\begin{split}\frac{\partial f_{i}(\bm{x})}{\partial\bm{x}_{i}}&=\frac{1}{n}\biggl(\frac{\partial}{\partial\bm{x}_{i}}V\Big(\sum_{j=1}^{n}\bm{x}_{j}\Big)-\frac{\partial}{\partial\bm{x}_{i}}V\Big(\bm{x}_{i}\bm{x}_{i}^{T}V\sum_{j=1}^{n}\bm{x}_{j}\Big)\biggl)\\ &\!\!\!\!=\frac{1}{n}\biggl(V-\bm{x}_{i}^{T}V\sum_{j=1}^{n}\bm{x}_{j}I-\bm{x}_{i}\Big(\bm{x}_{i}^{T}V+\sum_{j=1}^{n}\bm{x}_{j}^{T}V\Big)\biggl).\end{split}

For the off-diagonal terms, instead we have

∂fi​(𝒙)∂𝒙h=1n​(I−𝒙i​𝒙iT)​V​∂∂𝒙h​∑j=1n𝒙j.\frac{\partial f_{i}(\bm{x})}{\partial\bm{x}_{h}}=\frac{1}{n}(I-\bm{x}_{i}\bm{x}_{i}^{T})V\frac{\partial}{\partial\bm{x}_{h}}\sum_{j=1}^{n}\bm{x}_{j}.
 

The linearization can be used to determine the local stability character of the equilibria of (5).

Lemma 4

The consensus point 𝐱i=𝐯1\bm{x}_{i}=\bm{v}_{1} ∀i\forall\,i is locally asymptotically stable for (5), while the remaining consensus equilibria 𝐱i=𝐯k\bm{x}_{i}=\bm{v}_{k} ∀i\forall\,i, with k=2,…,dk=2,\ldots,d, are all unstable. At a consensus equilibrium 𝐯k\bm{v}_{k}, the eigenvalues of F⁡(𝐯k)F(\bm{v}_{k}) are

  1. 1.

    −2​λk-2\lambda_{k} of multiplicity nn,

  2. 2.

    λh−λk\lambda_{h}-\lambda_{k}, for h=1,…,k−1,k+1,…,dh=1,\ldots,k-1,k+1,\ldots,d,

  3. 3.

    −λk-\lambda_{k} of multiplicity n​d−n−d+1nd-n-d+1.

The bipartite consensus and polygonal equilibria are all unstable.

Proof.

To prove this lemma, we follow the same procedure of Lemma 10 of [33]. Remarkably, our system (5) and the (different) system in [33] share the same eigenvectors even though they have different eigenvalues. Notice first that, when computed in an eigenvector 𝒗k\bm{v}_{k}, the Jacobian of (5) can be compactly expressed using tensor products as

F⁡(𝒗k)=∂f⁡(𝒙)∂𝒙|𝒙i=𝒗k=1n​𝟙𝟙T⊗(I−𝒗k​𝒗kT)​V−I⊗(𝒗kT​V​𝒗k​I+𝒗k​𝒗kT​V).\begin{split}&F(\bm{v}_{k})=\left.\frac{\partial f(\bm{x})}{\partial\bm{x}}\right|_{\bm{x}_{i}=\bm{v}_{k}}\\ &=\frac{1}{n}\mathds{1}\mathds{1}^{T}\otimes\left(I-\bm{v}_{k}\bm{v}_{k}^{T}\right)V-I\otimes\left(\bm{v}_{k}^{T}V\bm{v}_{k}I+\bm{v}_{k}\bm{v}_{k}^{T}V\right).\end{split} (7)

The first term represents a factor present in all entries of FF, while the second one is present only on the diagonal. For F⁡(𝒗k)F(\bm{v}_{k}) there are 3 classes of eigenvectors:

  1. 1.

    The first class is given by 𝒑ℓ=[0​…​ 0⏟ℓ−1​𝒗kT​0​…​ 0⏟n−ℓ]T\bm{p}^{\ell}=[\,\underbrace{0\,\ldots\,0}_{\ell-1}\,\bm{v}_{k}^{T}\,\underbrace{0\,\ldots\,0}_{n-\ell}\,]^{T}. There are nn such eigenvectors, and they are obviously all orthogonal to each other. Since

    (I−𝒗k​𝒗kT)​V​𝒗k=λk​(𝒗k−𝒗k​𝒗kT​𝒗k)=0,(I-\bm{v}_{k}\bm{v}_{k}^{T})V\bm{v}_{k}=\lambda_{k}(\bm{v}_{k}-\bm{v}_{k}\bm{v}_{k}^{T}\bm{v}_{k})=0,

    and

    (𝒗kT​V​𝒗k​I+𝒗k​𝒗kT​V)​𝒗k=λk​(𝒗kT​𝒗k​𝒗k+𝒗k​𝒗kT​𝒗k)=2​λk​𝒗k,\begin{split}(\bm{v}_{k}^{T}V\bm{v}_{k}I+\bm{v}_{k}\bm{v}_{k}^{T}V)\bm{v}_{k}&=\lambda_{k}(\bm{v}_{k}^{T}\bm{v}_{k}\bm{v}_{k}+\bm{v}_{k}\bm{v}_{k}^{T}\bm{v}_{k})\\ &=2\lambda_{k}\bm{v}_{k},\end{split}

    it is

    F(𝒗k)𝒑ℓ=−2λk𝒑ℓ,ℓ=1,…,n,F(\bm{v}_{k})\bm{p}^{\ell}=-2\lambda_{k}\bm{p}^{\ell},\quad\ell=1,\ldots,n,

    i.e., 𝒑ℓ\bm{p}^{\ell} is an eigenvector of F⁡(𝒗k)F(\bm{v}_{k}) of eigenvalue −2​λk-2\lambda_{k}.

  2. 2.

    The second class of eigenvectors is given by 𝒒h=[𝒗hT…𝒗hT]T\bm{q}^{h}=\begin{bmatrix}\bm{v}_{h}^{T}&\ldots&\bm{v}_{h}^{T}\end{bmatrix}^{T}, where 𝒗h\bm{v}_{h} is an eigenvector of VV associated to λh\lambda_{h} with h≠kh\neq k, so that 𝒗kT​𝒗h=0\bm{v}_{k}^{T}\bm{v}_{h}=0. There are d−1d-1 such 𝒒h\bm{q}^{h} vectors. Computing

    (I−𝒗k​𝒗kT)​V​𝒗h=λh​(𝒗h−𝒗k​𝒗kT​𝒗h)=λh​𝒗h(I-\bm{v}_{k}\bm{v}_{k}^{T})V\bm{v}_{h}=\lambda_{h}(\bm{v}_{h}-\bm{v}_{k}\bm{v}_{k}^{T}\bm{v}_{h})=\lambda_{h}\bm{v}_{h}
    (𝒗kT​V​𝒗k​I+𝒗k​𝒗kT​V)​𝒗h=λk​𝒗kT​𝒗k​𝒗h+λh​𝒗k​𝒗kT​𝒗h=λk​𝒗h,\begin{split}(\bm{v}_{k}^{T}V\bm{v}_{k}I+\bm{v}_{k}\bm{v}_{k}^{T}V)\bm{v}_{h}&=\lambda_{k}\bm{v}_{k}^{T}\bm{v}_{k}\bm{v}_{h}+\lambda_{h}\bm{v}_{k}\bm{v}_{k}^{T}\bm{v}_{h}\\ &=\lambda_{k}\bm{v}_{h},\end{split}

    hence

    F(𝒗k)𝒒h=(λh−λk)𝒒h,h=1,…,k−1,k+1,…,d.\!\!\!\!F(\bm{v}_{k})\bm{q}^{h}=(\lambda_{h}-\lambda_{k})\bm{q}^{h},\;\;h=1,\ldots,k-1,k+1,\ldots,d.

    The remaining n​d−n−d+1nd-n-d+1 eigenvectors are assembled by considering vectors 𝒓=[(𝒛1)T(𝒛2)T…(𝒛n)T]T\bm{r}=\begin{bmatrix}(\bm{z}^{1})^{T}&(\bm{z}^{2})^{T}&\ldots&(\bm{z}^{n})^{T}\end{bmatrix}^{T} s.t. 𝒗kT​𝒛i=0\bm{v}_{k}^{T}\bm{z}^{i}=0 and 𝒗hT​𝒛i=0\bm{v}_{h}^{T}\bm{z}^{i}=0 for all i=1,…,ni=1,\ldots,n and all h=1,…,k−1,k+1,…,dh=1,\ldots,k-1,k+1,\ldots,d. Since the number of such constraints is d−1+nd-1+n, there exist n​d−n−d+1nd-n-d+1 such vectors 𝒓\bm{r}. Notice that the 𝒛i\bm{z}^{i} can always be chosen so that ∑i=1n𝒛i=0\sum_{i=1}^{n}\bm{z}^{i}=0. Computing

    (I−𝒗k​𝒗kT)​V​𝒛i=V​𝒛i−λk​𝒗k​𝒗kT​𝒛i=V​𝒛i(I-\bm{v}_{k}\bm{v}_{k}^{T})V\bm{z}^{i}=V\bm{z}^{i}-\lambda_{k}\bm{v}_{k}\bm{v}_{k}^{T}\bm{z}^{i}=V\bm{z}^{i}
    (𝒗kT​V​𝒗k​I+𝒗k​𝒗kT​V)​𝒛i=λk​𝒗kT​𝒗k​𝒛i+λk​𝒗k​𝒗kT​𝒛i=λk​𝒛i,\begin{split}(\bm{v}_{k}^{T}V\bm{v}_{k}I+\bm{v}_{k}\bm{v}_{k}^{T}V)\bm{z}^{i}&=\lambda_{k}\bm{v}_{k}^{T}\bm{v}_{k}\bm{z}^{i}+\lambda_{k}\bm{v}_{k}\bm{v}_{k}^{T}\bm{z}_{i}\\ &=\lambda_{k}\bm{z}^{i},\end{split}

When k>1k>1, then at least one of the eigenvalues of the second class is λ1−λk>0\lambda_{1}-\lambda_{k}>0, hence the equilibrium 𝒗k\bm{v}_{k} is unstable. When k=1k=1, as by assumption λ1>0\lambda_{1}>0 and λ1>λk\lambda_{1}>\lambda_{k} for all k=2,…,dk=2,\ldots,d, all eigenvalues of F⁡(𝒗1)F(\bm{v}_{1}) are negative, meaning that 𝒗1\bm{v}_{1} is locally asymptotically stable for (5).

Consider now a bipartite consensus point 𝒙i=±𝒗k\bm{x}_{i}=\pm\bm{v}_{k}. Assume that n1n_{1} agents are equal to 𝒗k\bm{v}_{k} and n2=n−n1n_{2}=n-n_{1} agent to −𝒗k-\bm{v}_{k}. Denote 𝒱1\mathcal{V}_{1} and 𝒱2\mathcal{V}_{2} the associated sets of indices. In the Jacobian matrix F⁡(𝒙)F(\bm{x}) computed at such bipartite consensus we have now the following cases:

  • •

    if i∈𝒱1i\in\mathcal{V}_{1} and h=ih=i:

  • •

i.e., some of the diagonal terms switch sign. In compact form, assuming that the first n1n_{1} indices are in 𝒱1\mathcal{V}_{1} and the remaining n2n_{2} in 𝒱2\mathcal{V}_{2},

F(𝒗k)=1n𝟙𝟙T⊗(I−𝒗k𝒗kT)V−n1−n2n⋅⋅diag⁡[1​…​ 1⏟n1​times​−1​…−1⏟n2​times]⊗(𝒗kT​V​𝒗k​I+𝒗k​𝒗kT​V).\begin{split}&F(\bm{v}_{k})=\frac{1}{n}\mathds{1}\mathds{1}^{T}\otimes\left(I-\bm{v}_{k}\bm{v}_{k}^{T}\right)V-\frac{n_{1}-n_{2}}{n}\cdot\\ &\;\cdot{\rm diag}[\underbrace{1\;\ldots\;1}_{n_{1}\;\text{times}}\underbrace{-1\;\ldots\;-1}_{n_{2}\;\text{times}}]\otimes\left(\bm{v}_{k}^{T}V\bm{v}_{k}I+\bm{v}_{k}\bm{v}_{k}^{T}V\right).\end{split}

F⁡(𝒗k)​𝒑ℓ={−2​(n1−n2)n​λk​𝒑ℓif ​k∈𝒱12​(n1−n2)n​λk​𝒑ℓif ​k∈𝒱2.F(\bm{v}_{k})\bm{p}^{\ell}=\begin{cases}-\frac{2(n_{1}-n_{2})}{n}\lambda_{k}\bm{p}^{\ell}&\text{if }\;k\in\mathcal{V}_{1}\\ \frac{2(n_{1}-n_{2})}{n}\lambda_{k}\bm{p}^{\ell}&\text{if }\;k\in\mathcal{V}_{2}.\end{cases}

Regardless of the sign of λk\lambda_{k} and of the cardinality of the 𝒱1/𝒱2\mathcal{V}_{1}/\mathcal{V}_{2} partition, the bipartite consensus point is always unstable, since both ±2​(n1−n2)n​λk\pm\frac{2(n_{1}-n_{2})}{n}\lambda_{k} are eigenvalues.

𝒖˙i=1n​(I−(𝒔i+𝒖i)​(𝒔i+𝒖i)T)​V​∑j=1n(𝒔j+𝒖j)≈1n​(I−𝒔i​𝒔iT)​V​∑j=1n𝒔j⏟=0+(I−𝒔i​𝒔iT)​V​∑j=1n𝒖j−(𝒖i​𝒔iT+𝒔i​𝒖iT)​V​∑j=1n𝒔j⏟=0+h.o.t.\begin{split}\dot{\bm{u}}_{i}&=\frac{1}{n}\left(I-(\bm{s}_{i}+\bm{u}_{i})(\bm{s}_{i}+\bm{u}_{i})^{T}\right)V\sum_{j=1}^{n}(\bm{s}_{j}+\bm{u}_{j})\\ &\approx\frac{1}{n}\left(I-\bm{s}_{i}\bm{s}_{i}^{T}\right)\underbrace{V\sum_{j=1}^{n}\bm{s}_{j}}_{=0}+\left(I-\bm{s}_{i}\bm{s}_{i}^{T}\right)V\sum_{j=1}^{n}\bm{u}_{j}\\ &\;\;-(\bm{u}_{i}\bm{s}_{i}^{T}+\bm{s}_{i}\bm{u}_{i}^{T})\underbrace{V\sum_{j=1}^{n}\bm{s}_{j}}_{=0}+h.o.t.\end{split}

Recall that VV has always at least one positive eigenvalue λ1>0\lambda_{1}>0. We can always choose 𝒖\bm{u} s.t. each 𝒖j\bm{u}_{j} has a nonzero component in the direction of the associated eigenvector 𝒗1\bm{v}_{1}: expanding in the eigenbasis of VV, 𝒖j=∑k=1dηkj​𝒗k\bm{u}_{j}=\sum_{k=1}^{d}\eta^{j}_{k}\bm{v}_{k} with η1j≠0\eta^{j}_{1}\neq 0. If 𝒔i=∑k=1dζki​𝒗k\bm{s}_{i}=\sum_{k=1}^{d}\zeta^{i}_{k}\bm{v}_{k}, and using orthogonality,

𝒖˙i=∑kη˙ki​𝒗k=1n((I−∑kζik𝒗k∑ℓζiℓ𝒗ℓT)V∑j∑kηjk𝒗k)=1n((I−∑kζik𝒗k∑ℓζiℓ𝒗ℓT)∑j∑kηjkλk𝒗k)=1n(∑j,kηjkλk𝒗k−∑kζik𝒗k∑ℓζiℓλℓ∑jηjℓ)\begin{split}\dot{\bm{u}}_{i}&=\sum_{k}\dot{\eta}^{i}_{k}\bm{v}_{k}\\ &=\frac{1}{n}\biggl(\Big(I-\sum_{k}\zeta^{i}_{k}\bm{v}_{k}\sum_{\ell}\zeta^{i}_{\ell}\bm{v}_{\ell}^{T}\Big)V\sum_{j}\sum_{k}\eta^{j}_{k}\bm{v}_{k}\biggl)\\ &=\frac{1}{n}\biggl(\Big(I-\sum_{k}\zeta^{i}_{k}\bm{v}_{k}\sum_{\ell}\zeta^{i}_{\ell}\bm{v}_{\ell}^{T}\Big)\sum_{j}\sum_{k}\eta^{j}_{k}\lambda_{k}\bm{v}_{k}\biggl)\\ &=\frac{1}{n}\biggl(\sum_{j,k}\eta^{j}_{k}\lambda_{k}\bm{v}_{k}-\sum_{k}\zeta^{i}_{k}\bm{v}_{k}\sum_{\ell}\zeta^{i}_{\ell}\lambda_{\ell}\sum_{j}\eta^{j}_{\ell}\biggl)\end{split}

or, projecting along 𝒗1\bm{v}_{1},

η˙1i=1n(∑jη1jλ1−ζ1i∑ℓζℓiλℓ∑jηℓj).\dot{\eta}^{i}_{1}=\frac{1}{n}\biggl(\sum_{j}\eta^{j}_{1}\lambda_{1}-\zeta^{i}_{1}\sum_{\ell}\zeta^{i}_{\ell}\lambda_{\ell}\sum_{j}\eta^{j}_{\ell}\biggl).

To conclude the argument, it is enough to show that instability occurs along a specific 𝒖\bm{u}. One such direction is 𝒖\bm{u} that perturbs 𝒔\bm{s} only along the first eigenvector 𝒗1\bm{v}_{1} for each i=1,…,ni=1,\ldots,n, i.e., for all ii, η1i≠0\eta^{i}_{1}\neq 0 and ηki=0\eta^{i}_{k}=0 for k=2,…,dk=2,\ldots,d. In this case in fact we get

η˙1i=1n​(1−(ζ1i)2)​λ1​∑jη1j,\dot{\eta}^{i}_{1}=\frac{1}{n}\left(1-(\zeta^{i}_{1})^{2}\right)\lambda_{1}\sum_{j}\eta^{j}_{1},

or, in vector form (collecting only the η1i\eta^{i}_{1} components, 𝜼1=[η11…η1n]T\bm{\eta}_{1}=\begin{bmatrix}\eta^{1}_{1}&\ldots&\eta^{n}_{1}\end{bmatrix}^{T}),

𝜼˙1=λ1n​(I−Ψ12)​𝟙𝟙T​𝜼1\dot{\bm{\eta}}_{1}=\frac{\lambda_{1}}{n}\left(I-\Psi_{1}^{2}\right)\mathds{1}\mathds{1}^{T}\bm{\eta}_{1}

where Ψ1=diag⁡(ζ11,…,ζ1n)\Psi_{1}={\rm diag}(\zeta^{1}_{1},\ldots,\zeta^{n}_{1}). The matrix 𝟙𝟙T\mathds{1}\mathds{1}^{T} is a rank-1 matrix of eigenvalues 11 and 00, while |ζ1i|<1|\zeta^{i}_{1}|<1 because 𝒔\bm{s} is not an eigenvector of VV, hence I−Ψ12≻0I-\Psi_{1}^{2}\succ 0. Since λ1>0\lambda_{1}>0, the matrix λ1n​(I−Ψ12)​𝟙𝟙T\frac{\lambda_{1}}{n}\left(I-\Psi_{1}^{2}\right)\mathds{1}\mathds{1}^{T} has at least one positive eigenvalue, hence 𝒔\bm{s} is an unstable equilibrium for (5).  

Finally, the following lemma shows that a Lyapunov stability argument can be set up for (5).

Lemma 5

The function W⁡(𝐱)=12​(λ1−1n​∑j=1n𝐱jT​V​∑j=1n𝐱j)W(\bm{x})=\frac{1}{2}\left(\lambda_{1}-\frac{1}{n}\sum_{j=1}^{n}\bm{x}_{j}^{T}V\sum_{j=1}^{n}\bm{x}_{j}\right) is a Lyapunov function for (5) and guarantees that (5) converges to one of the equilibria determined in Lemma 2.

Proof.

Consider 𝒎=𝒎⁡(𝒙)=1n​∑j=1n𝒙j\bm{m}=\bm{m}(\bm{x})=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{j=1}^{n}\bm{x}_{j} and 𝒚=V​𝒎\bm{y}=V\bm{m}. Differentiating W⁡(𝒙)=12​(λ1−1n​𝒎T​V​𝒎)W(\bm{x})=\frac{1}{2}\left(\lambda_{1}-\frac{1}{n}\bm{m}^{T}V\bm{m}\right) gives

W˙​(𝒙)=−1n𝒎TV∑i=1n(I−𝒙i𝒙iT)V𝒎=−nn​𝒎T​V​V​𝒎+1n​𝒎T​V​∑i=1n𝒙i​𝒙iT​V​𝒎=−𝒚T​𝒚+1n​𝒚T​∑i=1n𝒙i​𝒙iT​𝒚≤−‖𝒚‖2+1n​μmax​[∑i=1n𝒙i​𝒙iT]​‖𝒚‖2=(−1+nn)​‖𝒚‖2=0\begin{split}\dot{W}(\bm{x})&=-\frac{1}{n}\bm{m}^{T}V\sum_{i=1}^{n}(I-\bm{x}_{i}\bm{x}_{i}^{T})V\bm{m}\\ &=-\frac{n}{n}\bm{m}^{T}VV\bm{m}+\frac{1}{n}\bm{m}^{T}V\sum_{i=1}^{n}\bm{x}_{i}\bm{x}_{i}^{T}V\bm{m}\\ &=-\bm{y}^{T}\bm{y}+\frac{1}{n}\bm{y}^{T}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\bm{x}_{i}\bm{x}_{i}^{T}\bm{y}\\ &\leq-\|\bm{y}\|^{2}+\frac{1}{n}\mu_{\max}\left[\sum_{i=1}^{n}\bm{x}_{i}\bm{x}_{i}^{T}\right]\|\bm{y}\|^{2}\\ &=\left(-1+\frac{n}{n}\right)\|\bm{y}\|^{2}=0\end{split}

where we have used that each psd matrix 𝒙i​𝒙iT⪯I\bm{x}_{i}\bm{x}_{i}^{T}\preceq I since it projects onto the direction 𝒙i\bm{x}_{i}, and hence 0⪯∑i=1n𝒙i​𝒙iT⪯n​I0\preceq\sum_{i=1}^{n}\bm{x}_{i}\bm{x}_{i}^{T}\preceq nI, from which 0≤μk​[∑i=1n𝒙i​𝒙iT]≤n0\leq\mu_{k}\left[\sum_{i=1}^{n}\bm{x}_{i}\bm{x}_{i}^{T}\right]\leq n for all eigenvalues of ∑i=1n𝒙i​𝒙iT\sum_{i=1}^{n}\bm{x}_{i}\bm{x}_{i}^{T}.

Since the state space is compact, trajectories exist for all tt and have limit points. Hence LaSalle’s invariance principle applies. In particular, trajectories converge to the largest invariant set contained in

ℒ={𝒙∈(𝕊d−1)n s. t. W˙(𝒙)=0}={𝒚 s. t. n∥𝒚∥2=∑i=1n(𝒙iT𝒚)2}.\begin{split}\mathcal{L}&=\{\bm{x}\in(\mathbb{S}^{d-1})^{n}\;\text{ s. t. }\;\dot{W}(\bm{x})=0\}\\ &=\{\bm{y}\;\text{ s. t. }\;n\|\bm{y}\|^{2}=\sum_{i=1}^{n}(\bm{x}_{i}^{T}\bm{y})^{2}\}.\end{split}

For the system (5), 𝒙∈ℒ\bm{x}\in\mathcal{L} when 𝒚=0\bm{y}=0 or, from the calculations above for W˙\dot{W}, when equality holds in μmax​[∑i=1n𝒙i​𝒙iT]≤n\mu_{\max}\left[\sum_{i=1}^{n}\bm{x}_{i}\bm{x}_{i}^{T}\right]\leq n, i.e., when all 𝒙i\bm{x}_{i} are collinear: 𝒙i=±𝒗\bm{x}_{i}=\pm\bm{v} for some 𝒗\bm{v}. In fact, in this case, ∑i=1n𝒙i​𝒙iT=n​𝒗​𝒗T\sum_{i=1}^{n}\bm{x}_{i}\bm{x}_{i}^{T}=n\bm{v}\bm{v}^{T}. If 𝒗=𝒗k\bm{v}=\bm{v}_{k} for some k=1,…,dk=1,\ldots,d, then we have an invariant point. If instead 𝒗≠𝒗k\bm{v}\neq\bm{v}_{k}, k=1,…,dk=1,\ldots,d (i.e., the consensus point is not an equilibrium), then it is 𝒙˙i|𝒙i=𝒗=(I−𝒗​𝒗T)​V​𝒗=𝒙˙j|𝒙j=𝒗≠0\left.\dot{\bm{x}}_{i}\right|_{\bm{x}_{i}=\bm{v}}=(I-\bm{v}\bm{v}^{T})V\bm{v}=\left.\dot{\bm{x}}_{j}\right|_{\bm{x}_{j}=\bm{v}}\neq 0, for all i,ji,j, and the dynamics become nn identical copies of the Oja flow (2). From Lemma 1, all these nn copies converge to ±𝒗k\pm\bm{v}_{k} for some kk (almost always to ±𝒗1\pm\bm{v}_{1}). Summarizing, the largest invariant set in ℒ\mathcal{L} is given by the set of equilibria of (5), hence all trajectories of (5) converge to one of the equilibria in ℒ\mathcal{L} computed in Lemma 2.  

Proof of Theorem 1. From Lemma 5 all trajectories converge to one of the equilibria computed in Lemma 2. Lemma 4 says that only the consensus point 𝒗1\bm{v}_{1} corresponding to the principal eigenvalue of VV is locally asymptotically stable, while all other equilibria are unstable. Since all trajectories of (5) have a limit point, generically such limit point must be 𝒗1\bm{v}_{1}.  

Remark 2

Even though all equilibria except one (or one pair, if one counts also the antipodal point) are unstable, they typically have a basin of attraction associated to a stable submanifold. These stable submanifolds are however necessarily of measure 0 in (𝕊d−1)n(\mathbb{S}^{d-1})^{n}, and hence so must be the basins of attraction of the unstable equilibria.

5 Self-Attention dynamics

The self-attention system (1) differs from (5) in the fact that in the right hand side of the ODEs, the average of the states of the nn agents, 1n​∑j=1n𝒙j\frac{1}{n}\sum_{j=1}^{n}\bm{x}_{j}, is replaced by a weighted average 𝒎=1n​∑j=1nAi​j​(𝒙)​𝒙j\bm{m}=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{j=1}^{n}A_{ij}(\bm{x})\bm{x}_{j}, with (state-dependent) weights given by the attention coefficients.

5.1 Equilibria

Apart from the three classes of equilibria already obtained for the multiagent Oja flow, in the self-attention dynamics we have an extra class, due to the fact that the total influence on agent ii of all other agents 𝒚i=𝒚i​(𝒙)=V​∑j=1nAi​j​(𝒙)​𝒙j\bm{y}_{i}=\bm{y}_{i}(\bm{x})=V\sum_{j=1}^{n}A_{ij}(\bm{x})\bm{\bm{x}}_{j} now differs from agent to agent.

Lemma 6

The system (1) has the following classes of equilibria

  1. 1.

    consensus: 𝒙i=𝒗k\bm{x}_{i}=\bm{v}_{k} ∀i\forall\,i, and k=1,…,dk=1,\ldots,d;

  2. 2.

    bipartite consensus: 𝒙i=±𝒗k\bm{x}_{i}=\pm\bm{v}_{k} ∀i\forall\,i and k=1,…,dk=1,\ldots,d;

  3. 3.

    polygonal equilibria: {𝒙i∈𝕊d−1s.t.V∑j=1nAi​j(𝒙)𝒙j=0}\{\bm{x}_{i}\in\mathbb{S}^{d-1}\;\text{s.t.}\;V\sum_{j=1}^{n}A_{ij}(\bm{x})\bm{x}_{j}=0\}, i=1,…,ni=1,\ldots,n;

  4. 4.

    clustering equilibria: {𝒙i∈𝕊d−1s.t.γi𝒙i=V∑j=1nAi​j(𝒙)𝒙j}\{\bm{x}_{i}\in\mathbb{S}^{d-1}\;\text{s.t.}\;\gamma_{i}\bm{x}_{i}=V\sum_{j=1}^{n}A_{ij}(\bm{x})\bm{x}_{j}\} for some scalars γi\gamma_{i}, i=1,…,ni=1,\ldots,n, k=1,…,dk=1,\ldots,d.

Proof.

For the first three cases, the proof is identical to that of Lemma 2, provided that 𝒚\bm{y} is replaced by 𝒚i=∑j=1nAi​j​(𝒙)​V​𝒙j\bm{y}_{i}=\sum_{j=1}^{n}A_{ij}(\bm{x})V\bm{\bm{x}}_{j}. Concerning the clustering equilibria, these correspond to 𝒚i∈ker⁡(I−𝒙i​𝒙iT)\bm{y}_{i}\in\ker(I-\bm{x}_{i}\bm{x}_{i}^{T}), or, equivalently, 𝒚i\bm{y}_{i} aligned with 𝒙i\bm{x}_{i}, i=1,…,ni=1,\ldots,n but not necessarily aligned with an eigenvector 𝒗k\bm{v}_{k}, i.e., 𝒚i=γi​𝒙i\bm{y}_{i}=\gamma_{i}\bm{x}_{i} for some scalar γi\gamma_{i}, but possibly 𝒚i∦𝒗k\bm{y}_{i}\nparallel\bm{v}_{k} ∀k\forall\,k.  

Remark 3

Clustering equilibria own their name to the fact that typically multiple agents are found at the same value. In particular we say that 𝒙1,…,𝒙n\bm{x}_{1},\ldots,\bm{x}_{n} are at an mm-clustering equilibrium point if 𝒙i∈{𝒘1,…,𝒘m}\bm{x}_{i}\in\{\bm{w}_{1},\ldots,\bm{w}_{m}\} with 1≤m≤n1\leq m\leq n, i.e., if 𝒙1,…,𝒙n\bm{x}_{1},\ldots,\bm{x}_{n} cluster at the mm vectors 𝒘1,…,𝒘m\bm{w}_{1},\ldots,\bm{w}_{m}. Notice that some 𝒘i\bm{w}_{i} can be eigenvectors of VV.

Remark 4

A clustering equilibrium can be a consensus, i.e, 𝒙i=𝒙j\bm{x}_{i}=\bm{x}_{j} for all i,ji,j, but with 𝒙i\bm{x}_{i} which is not aligned with any eigenvector of VV, i.e., 𝒙i∦𝒗k\bm{x}_{i}\nparallel\bm{v}_{k} ∀k\forall\,k. We refer to these as 1-clustering, while the “consensus” characterization is reserved for the case 𝒙i|𝒗k\bm{x}_{i}\parallel\bm{v}_{k}. A 2-clustering instead typically is s.t. 𝒙i∈{𝒘1,𝒘2}\bm{x}_{i}\in\{\bm{w}_{1},\bm{w}_{2}\} ∀i\forall\,i, with 𝒘1≠−𝒘2\bm{w}_{1}\neq-\bm{w}_{2}.

Proposition 1

The system (1) has clustering equilibria iff ∃\exists scalars γ1,…,γn\gamma_{1},\ldots,\gamma_{n} s.t. the matrix (In⊗Id−(Γ⊗Id)​(A⁡(𝐱)⊗Id)​(In⊗V))(I_{n}\otimes I_{d}-(\Gamma\otimes I_{d})(A(\bm{x})\otimes I_{d})(I_{n}\otimes V)) is singular, where Γ=diag⁡(γ1,…,γn)\Gamma={\rm diag}(\gamma_{1},\ldots,\gamma_{n}).

In vector form, the clustering equilibrium condition 𝒙i=γi​V​∑j=1nAi​j​(𝒙)​𝒙j\bm{x}_{i}=\gamma_{i}V\sum_{j=1}^{n}A_{ij}(\bm{x})\bm{\bm{x}}_{j} becomes 𝒙=(Γ⊗Id)​(A⁡(𝒙)⊗Id)​(In⊗V)​𝒙\bm{x}=(\Gamma\otimes I_{d})(A(\bm{x})\otimes I_{d})(I_{n}\otimes V)\bm{x}, where 𝒙T=[𝒙1T​…​𝒙nT]\bm{x}^{T}=[\bm{x}_{1}^{T}\,\ldots\,\bm{x}_{n}^{T}]. Rewriting it as (In⊗Id−(Γ⊗Id)​(A⁡(𝒙)⊗Id)​(In⊗V
